overview: The Buyids were a Daylamite ruling family whose related principalities dominated much of Iran and Iraq in the tenth and eleventh centuries. The two imported map labels share this history, but their dates and outlines contain serious errors explained below.

periods.title: Power in Baghdad
periods.summary: Buyid rulers controlled the Abbasid capital.

periods.title: The remaining southern territories
periods.summary: Power in Fars ended amid regional conquests.

sections.title: A ruling family and its subjects

items.text: The Buwayhid Emirates outline in 1000 broadly covers Iran and Iraq, but its repeated appearance in 1200 is too late. The Buyid dynasty label has a different, misplaced 1200 outline around Afghanistan and Pakistan. Neither record establishes accurate borders; both extend to 1279, long after Buyid power ended. These cards describe the historical dynasty.

The founding brothers, Ali, Hasan and Ahmad, built related principalities rather than one consistently united state. Their descendants competed over provinces and seniority. In 945 Ahmad entered Baghdad and received the title Muizz al-Dawla. The Abbasid caliph remained, while military and political power rested heavily with the Buyid rulers.

A silver dirham struck at Fasa in 959 or 960 names three authorities: the caliph al-Muti, Rukn al-Dawla and Adud al-Dawla. Their names fit on a coin less than three centimeters across. Money could carry a compact statement about layered authority, alongside the religious declarations familiar to those who handled it.

Buyid patronage supported Shiite scholars in Baghdad, especially around the commercial district of Karkh. The vizier Sabur ibn Ardashir established a major library there in 991 or 992. Sunni institutions and the Abbasid caliphate continued too. Religious life was diverse, and competition between communities could also produce serious tension and violence.

Governing involved offices as well as armies. Buyid administration retained finance, correspondence and military departments, drawing on Abbasid practice. Officials had to collect and account for revenue, transmit decisions and manage soldiers. A change of ruling family did not mean that every ledger, letter-writing practice or office was thrown away.

Royal households could shape government directly. After Fakhr al-Dawla died in 997, his widow Sayyeda governed Ray on behalf of their young son Majd al-Dawla. She came from the Bavandid ruling family. Her position shows a particular woman exercising political authority through dynastic relationships; it is not a description of every woman’s opportunities.

The Band-e Amir weir across the Kor River raised water for irrigation near Shiraz. Medieval accounts describe ten waterwheels lifting water to supply hundreds of villages. Stone blocks, mortar and masonry foundations formed a structure that also carried a bridge. It joined farming and transport in one engineering project; the surviving work also has a long history of repairs.

Adud al-Dawla built markets, caravanserais, cisterns and hospitals. The geographer Muqaddasi describes bazaars at Ramhormoz and a Shiraz palace with water channels and wind towers. These projects supplied places to trade, stay and store water. Their benefits depended on the work of builders, merchants, maintenance crews and water managers as well as royal funding.

At the new town of Kard-e Fanna Khusraw, two annual celebrations marked its foundation and the arrival of aqueduct water. Biruni reports the occasions, while another account links the idea to Nowruz celebrations Adud remembered from childhood in Isfahan. A reliable water supply was important enough to earn its own day of celebration.

sections.title: Homes, food and streets at Siraf

items.text: Siraf linked the Persian Gulf with Indian Ocean trade. Its excavated houses and pottery open a window onto life around the Buyid age, with some evidence also predating Buyid rule. Luxury imports mattered, but daily survival depended on water brought from surrounding mountains and food supplied from plains and valleys beyond them.

At Siraf, the excavators called one building House N. It had nine ground-floor rooms around a courtyard and evidence of an upper floor. The whole building occupied only about half the area of two larger neighboring houses. Families did not all inhabit one standard floor plan, even within the same excavated neighborhood.

Better houses had carved plaster decoration, including stars and rosettes. The excavator thought these might have stood over doors, but that placement was uncertain. Pieces fallen from upper stories also help archaeologists reconstruct buildings whose roofs and upper walls have vanished. A decorative fragment can reveal more about a home than an empty doorway.

Siraf’s roofs drained through earthenware pipes into stone-lined pits, often beside the houses. Some pits also received household waste and may have received waste from latrines. The streets themselves were unpaved. These discoveries reveal practical efforts to handle rain and rubbish, while the possible connection to toilets remains an archaeological interpretation.

A British Museum catalogue group records cooking pots made in India and excavated at Siraf, including object 2007,6001.4038, dated to the ninth or tenth century. Long-distance connections could therefore reach the cooking equipment used in a coastal town. The catalogue tells us where this pot was made and found, but not whose dinner it cooked.

sections.title: Care, books and looking at the sky

items.text: The Adudi hospital in Baghdad was founded in 982. Ibn Marzuban, trained in religious law and the sciences, became a hospital superintendent as well as a judge. His exact clinical role is uncertain; his administrative work is clearer. Running a place for the sick required organization as well as people who knew treatments.

The physician al-Majusi dedicated his Complete Book of the Medical Art to Adud al-Dawla. He wanted better organization and fuller attention to anatomy and surgery than he found in an earlier medical compilation. A surviving copy at the National Library of Medicine was made in 1208, showing the work’s later use without pretending that this particular manuscript came from the Buyid court.

Adud al-Dawla studied Arabic and supported works on subjects including grammar, medicine, astronomy and geometry. Muqaddasi describes his large Shiraz library as having a separate list for each subject. Finding a book therefore involved some organization rather than rummaging through every volume. Royal patronage supported learned specialists, though it does not establish schooling for every child.

The astronomer al-Sufi worked closely with Buyid rulers. His Book of the Fixed Stars combined classical constellations, Arabic star traditions and his own observations. Drawings accompanied tables of individual stars, with coordinates calculated for 964. Readers could compare a pictured pattern with measured positions in the sky, turning familiar stars into material for careful observation and criticism.

An astrolabe made by al-Khujandi in 984 or 985 survives in Doha’s Museum of Islamic Art. Its rotating star map has 33 pointers, six shaped like birds’ beaks. Tiny metal birds could point to stars! The maker worked in Buyid court circles; the catalogue gives Ray or Baghdad as possible places of manufacture, rather than one certain workshop.

sections.title: Objects, discoveries and a written sample

items.text: A tenth-century gold ewer in the Smithsonian bears an inscription naming the Buyid prince Bakhtiyar. Its relief decoration required skilled metalworking. The museum judges the inscription apparently genuine but identifies the handle as a likely later addition and records debate about authenticity. This luxurious vessel belongs to elite consumption, not a reconstruction of an ordinary family’s table.

A textile associated with the label “Buyid” in the Metropolitan Museum illustrates the hazards of dating beautiful objects. The museum now dates textile 30.67 probably to the early twentieth century. It should not be used to reconstruct Buyid clothing. Historical detective work includes recognizing that an object’s apparent age may be misleading.

On the Fasa dirham, the Arabic words “الامير العدل” (al-amīr al-ʿadl) mean “the Just Amir”. They form part of Adud al-Dawla’s title in the reverse inscription. This sample follows the Ashmolean catalogue’s transcription of a coin dated 348 AH, or 959 to 960 CE. It shows Arabic lettering used to announce a ruler’s authority on an everyday medium of exchange.

ending.text: Seljuk entry into Baghdad in 1055 ended Buyid rule there. Remaining power in Fars was lost during subsequent struggles involving the Shabankara and Seljuks, by the early 1060s. The family’s political rule ended, while its cities, medical writings and scientific traditions continued under new rulers.
